question: In its recently adopted report on the implementation of territorial development, Parliament calls on the Commission to explore new ways to raise greater awareness of the inclusive participation of civil society and local and regional authorities.

It does so in the context of the use of ITI and CLLD instruments, even taking into consideration the earmarking of a percentage to be used in post‑2027 cohesion policy in the case of these instruments. As a supporter of community-led local development, I welcome this position and ask the Commission whether the proposed earmarking of a percentage also seems desirable from its point of view.
I am also interested – although I am aware of the obstacles that exist – at what level this percentage might be.
answer: The bottom-up approach of Cohesion Policy has been further strengthened in the 2021-2027 programmes by introducing Policy Objective 5 ‘Europe closer to citizens’, which encompasses several instruments to support integrated territorial and local development strategies at sub-regional level.

The use of integrated territorial instruments is compulsory for urban development strategies, for which at least 8% of the European Regional Development Fund’s resources need to be allocated. Urban strategies also promote urban-rural linkages using a functional urban area approach.

Almost all Member States have programmed support for place-based investments under the above objective (EUR 19 billion) and 20 Member States use Integrated Territorial Investments with EUR 23 billion planned support mostly in functional urban areas, in cities and urban neighbourhoods, rural areas, mountain and island regions.

About half the Member States plan to support Community-Led Local Development with more than EUR 1.6 billion. 19 Member States have planned more than EUR 14 billion for ‘other territorial tools’ implemented in urban and rural areas. The above shows that even in the absence of specific earmarking, support for these place-based instruments is significant.
It is too early for the Commission to share a position on specific elements of the Cohesion Policy framework for post-2027.

The Commission is engaged in listening to all stakeholders through decentralised policy dialogues with the Member States, the European institutions, regional and local actors, and civil society, including a Group of high-level specialist s (1) to propose ways to improve the effectiveness and impact of Cohesion Policy. The group’s report has been published on 20 February 2024.
